questions.q: Why can SELECT * defeat a covering index?
options: It has no effect on which index gets used
SELECT * always causes a syntax error with indexes
If the index only includes certain columns but the query asks for all of them, SQL Server has to fall back to a Key Lookup or full scan
It automatically drops all indexes on the table
questions.explain: A narrow covering index only works if the query names just the columns the index actually contains.

questions.q: Why is a scalar UDF in a WHERE clause considered one of the worst anti-patterns?
options: It always returns incorrect results
It's invoked once per row (like a hidden cursor) and is also non-SARGable, so no index can help either
It automatically disables STATISTICS IO
It can only be used with CTEs
questions.explain: Scalar functions in predicates combine two problems: per-row execution overhead and blocking any index seek.

questions.q: What is the main problem with using a cursor to update rows one at a time?
options: Cursors are not supported in T-SQL
It abandons SQL Server's set-based processing strength, making it dramatically slower than an equivalent single UPDATE
Cursors can only read data, never write it
Cursors automatically lock the entire database
questions.explain: SQL Server is optimized to process whole sets of rows at once; row-by-row cursor processing gives up that advantage.

questions.q: What is an implicit conversion in a WHERE clause?
options: A conversion that only happens during backups
A feature that speeds up string comparisons
An automatic data-type conversion SQL Server performs when comparing mismatched types, which can prevent an index seek
A manual CAST the developer writes intentionally
questions.explain: Comparing an INT column to a string literal, for example, forces a conversion that can make the predicate non-SARGable.

questions.q: Per the Chapter 10 checklist, what should you check before declaring a query 'fast enough'?
options: Only whether it returns the correct number of rows
The actual execution plan and the logical reads, not just an assumption
Nothing — if it runs at all, it's fine
Only whether the query compiles without errors
questions.explain: Lessons 90 and 91 gave you the tools — plan shape and logical reads — to verify performance instead of guessing at it.
